07

Conclusion & real-world application

What this model is — and isn't — ready to do.

1

Logistic Regression is the stronger model, by a small margin

Both classifiers land close together, but Logistic Regression edges out Naive Bayes on every metric by learning a direct weight per word rather than assuming word independence.

2

68% accuracy on 3 balanced classes is a solid, honest result

Random guessing would score ~33%. The remaining errors cluster around the Neutral boundary and around negation, implicit sentiment, and mixed-clause reviews — real limits of a bag-of-words representation, not arbitrary mistakes.

3

Best used as a triage tool, not an autonomous judge

Flagging likely-negative reviews for a support team, tracking sentiment trend lines over time for a product line, or summarising aggregate opinion at scale are all strong fits — fully automated decisions on sarcastic or mixed-sentiment text are not, yet.

The Sentiment Lab — trained on an 18,000-review class-balanced sample drawn from 568,454 Amazon Fine Food Reviews. All charts and the prediction explorer read directly from the trained models' actual test-set output; nothing here is simulated.
